doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Improvising from age eight and learning jazz from records
summary: Levy says he improvised naturally as a child, learned jazz by listening and hearing live music, and his first jazz album was Coltrane's Crescent.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I wonder, this happened to me – getting in rock bands – and first I had an attitude. I mean I had been to music school and then I had an attitude, not a good one, about especially guitar players and so forth, people who were self-taught. And then – I felt like well they don’t know – you know I remember asking a guitar player once, that’s a great chord what is it? And he’d say it’s this. Like – and they I got over it because – I wonder if you had a similar experience where you realized that these ear players had something that you wanted as well?

Well I mean it’s a little different for me because I started improvising when I was eight. Okay? I just started making up my own music. It was just something that I did naturally and I didn’t understand where it was coming from but I would hear something and I would kind of imitate it, I mean I still do that now you know. And it was very hard for me to write out my improvisations because my musical being was really far ahead of my

ability to notate when I was eight and nine years old. I mean I could write out very rudimentary things. And my parents didn’t have a tape recorder so all that stuff that I would come home from school and sit at the piano for a half hour, it’s gone. I mean who knows what the heck it was. But there was one tune I wrote when I was eleven that I actually remembered and I actually still play today and I’ve recorded it on a few albums. But yeah, so it’s a complex question because being classically trained, I mean I knew a certain amount of theory and I knew some chord names, probably up to a ninth. Maybe I asked the guitar player, “What’s that chord?” “Oh it’s a ninth chord.” It’s like, “Okay, got it.” But a lot of what I did was just by intuition. And the way I learned how to play jazz was from listening to records and going to hear people play live at the Vanguard and places like that, you know, once I got into jazz, which is when I was 17 and 18, 17 I guess. And then I just immersed myself, I just – once I heard – the first jazz album I ever listened to was “Crescent.” Okay? That was it. Okay.
